6.1 Fund Types and Structures

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Stage 6 looks at how a US household can put the theory of the earlier stages into practice. Most household investing is done through funds, so this lesson looks at the kinds of funds and how they work; the next lesson looks at what they cost.

Open-end mutual funds

Section titled “Open-end mutual funds”

A mutual fund pools money from many investors and has a manager invest it according to a stated strategy. The most common kind is the open-end fund: the number of shares is not fixed, and investors can at any time buy new shares from the fund or sell shares back to it (redeem).

Purchases and redemptions take place at the net asset value (NAV):

NAV=A−LN\text{NAV} = \frac{A - L}{N}NAV=NA−L​

AAA is the value of the fund’s assets at closing prices, LLL its liabilities (for example fees owed), and NNN the number of shares. US mutual funds compute their NAV once each trading day at the close (4 p.m. Eastern time). By rule, orders to buy or redeem submitted before the close are filled at the NAV computed after that day’s close, which is called forward pricing; orders submitted after the close get the next trading day’s NAV.

By what they invest in, funds are stock funds, bond funds, balanced funds and money market funds. One fund often has several share classes, which invest in the same portfolio and differ only in how they charge fees (6.2 Fund Costs).

Check C1
An investor submits an order at 2 p.m. Eastern time to buy a US open-end stock fund, while the stock market is rising. His price is the fund's NAV computed at market prices as of 2 p.m.
How many times a day does a mutual fund compute its NAV, and when? Which NAV do orders submitted before the close get?

ETFs and creation and redemption

Section titled “ETFs and creation and redemption”

An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is also a fund holding a basket of assets, but its shares are listed on an exchange, and investors buy and sell them from each other at market prices at any time during trading hours, like stocks (3.1 Overview of the Financial System).

If an ETF’s price is set by buyers and sellers, why does it usually stay close to its NAV? The key is creation and redemption. Only large dealers called authorized participants (APs) can create or redeem shares directly with the ETF, usually in kind: an AP gives the ETF a basket of stocks matching the fund’s holdings and receives a large block (for example 50,000) of new ETF shares; this is a creation. Conversely, an AP hands back a block of ETF shares and receives a basket of stocks; this is a redemption. When the ETF’s market price moves away from the value of the basket, APs can buy and sell in the two markets and profit from the gap (arbitrage).

Check C2
A stock ETF's market price is 1% below the value of the basket of stocks it holds. How can an authorized participant profit, and with what result?
What value do you give up to create shares, and what do the shares sell for in the market? Is the ETF now dearer or cheaper than the basket?
In what form does the lesson say APs usually create and redeem? A cash redemption would make the fund sell and realize gains; how would that affect other holders?

Capital gains distributions and tax efficiency

Section titled “Capital gains distributions and tax efficiency”

In the US, when a mutual fund sells securities at a gain, the realized capital gains must be paid out to shareholders that year, and shareholders owe tax on them even if they have not sold any fund shares and reinvest the payout; this is a capital gains distribution. Mutual funds often realize capital gains because other investors redeem and the fund must sell securities to raise cash.

ETF redemptions are in kind: the fund does not sell stocks but hands them directly to the AP. Under US tax law, delivering securities in kind does not count as realizing a gain, and the fund can choose to hand over the shares with the lowest cost (the most unrealized gain). So when tracking the same index, an ETF rarely distributes capital gains, and most of its holders’ tax is deferred until they sell the ETF themselves.

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, both funds pay 15% tax on all gains, yet after 30 years the fund paying out capital gains each year ends clearly lower. The main reason is:
After the payout is taxed, the reinvested part raises the cost basis. Is that gain taxed again at the sale?
Do the two funds in the figure use the same tax rate?

Index funds

Section titled “Index funds”

An index fund does not pick securities; it holds the members of an index according to rules, aiming to earn the same return as the index. It can be a mutual fund or an ETF. The theoretical basis of index funds is the capital market line (4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line): hold the market portfolio (market portfolio) and adjust risk with the riskless asset.

Most broad indexes are weighted by market capitalization: each stock’s weight equals its market value as a share of the index’s total, as in the S&P 500 and the CRSP US Total Market Index, which covers the whole US stock market. Indexes also change their members from time to time, for example adding newly listed or grown companies and removing shrunken ones; index funds must then trade. There are also indexes weighted equally, by fundamental measures or by factors (4.6 Multifactor Models).

Check C4
A cap-weighted index fund must buy and sell stocks whenever the prices of the index members change, to keep the same weights as the index.
Suppose the fund holds a fixed fraction of each company's shares. When one stock rises, how do its weight in the index and its weight in the fund change?

Other fund structures

Section titled “Other fund structures”
  • A closed-end fund issues a fixed number of shares, which afterwards can only be bought and sold between investors on an exchange; the fund no longer creates or redeems shares.
  • Money market funds invest in short-term, high-quality debt (money market), aiming to keep the principal stable, and often serve as a substitute for cash.
  • Funds of funds invest in other funds. Target-date funds (target-date fund) are the most common kind: they hold a few stock and bond index funds and adjust the mix along a glide path.
Check C5
A closed-end fund's price can stay more than 10% below its NAV for years, while a large stock ETF's price rarely strays from NAV by more than a few tenths of a percent. The main reason is:
Riskier assets make the NAV itself swing more, but why would that keep the price below the value of those assets for years?
If rational investors could buy assets below value and cash in the gap, would the gap last? The key is whether it can be cashed in.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Open-end mutual funds are bought and redeemed at the NAV computed after that day’s close; one fund can have several share classes.
  • ETFs trade on exchanges at market prices; authorized participants create and redeem in kind, keeping the price close to NAV.
  • Mutual funds must pay out realized capital gains to shareholders, who pay the tax; ETFs redeem in kind and rarely distribute capital gains, so tax can be deferred until sale.
  • Index funds hold the members of an index by rule; broad indexes are mostly weighted by market capitalization.
  • Closed-end funds have a fixed number of shares that trade only on exchanges; money market funds substitute for cash; target-date funds are funds of funds.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
An investor puts 100,000 dollars in a taxable account for 20 years and can choose between two funds tracking the same index with the same fees: a mutual fund that each year pays out 5% of its NAV as long-term capital gains, with the investor paying the tax and reinvesting the rest; and an ETF that pays out no capital gains. Both funds earn a total return of 7% a year, the long-term capital gains tax rate is 15%, and everything is sold after 20 years.
(a) After selling at the end of 20 years and paying tax, how much is left in each case (thousand dollars)?
(b) His friend says: "Both funds' gains are taxed at 15%; one pays earlier and the other later, the total tax is about the same, so it makes no difference." Evaluate this statement, and say when the difference between the two becomes smaller.
Question 2
During the market turmoil of March 2020, some large corporate bond ETFs traded about 5% below their published NAV. The NAV of such an ETF is computed from a pricing service's estimates of each bond, and many corporate bonds barely traded in those days, with bid–ask spreads several times wider than usual.
(a) A commentator says: "The ETF is 5% cheaper than the assets it holds, which shows the ETF structure broke down in the crisis." Evaluate this statement: in those days, which was likely closer to the price at which investors could actually sell the bonds, the ETF price or the NAV?
(b) Why did authorized participants not close the 5% gap quickly? Under what conditions would the gap be a riskless arbitrage?
Question 3
A closed-end bond fund has a NAV of 20 dollars a share and a market price of 17 dollars. Each year it pays out 6% of NAV to shareholders, and its yearly expenses are 1.2% of NAV (already deducted before the payout).
(a) At the market price, what is the buyer's yearly payout rate?
(b) An investment newsletter says: "Buying a dollar of assets for 85 cents is an instant 15% gain." Evaluate this statement: when does the buyer actually get the 15%? If the discount stays at 15% forever, what is the benefit of buying at a discount?
Question 4
A market has only three stocks, A, B and C, with equal market values. Over a year A rises 50% and B and C are unchanged.
(a) At year end, how much of A (as a percentage of fund assets) must a cap-weighted index fund sell, and how much must a fund that rebalances to equal weights each year sell?
(b) An analyst says: "A cap-weighted index puts more of your money in the stocks that have risen most and are most expensive; an equal-weighted index is obviously better." Evaluate this statement.
